Exploring the Natural Wine Legacy of Jenny & François
Over 18 years, Jenny Lefcourt has helped shape America’s taste for natural wine
written by  
Kathleen Willcox
published
  
Photo by James Robinson Pictures.
Operating out of unofficial office spaces carved from their residences in France and New York City, Jenny Lefcourt and her husband, François Ecot, launched Jenny & François Selections as a side project in 2000 to import and distribute natural wines from France to a handful of New York restaurants and shops.
Ecot, who grew up on the outskirts of Paris, and whose family had a house in Burgundy, had studied winemaking in Beaune and was inspired by the new natural wine movement in French viticulture. Lefcourt wanted to use the nascent movement as a springboard for the import company while she was pursuing her Ph.D. in French cinema and literature at Harvard. By 2004, not long after completing her dissertation, Lefcourt had abandoned academia for the nomadic life of a wine-importing entrepreneur.
In the 18 years since it was created, the company has grown dramatically. Jenny & François now sells 279 wines from 71 producers in 10 countries to 42 states. The company distributes its own wines in New York, and sells the wine in its portfolio through other distributors throughout the rest of the country. Lefcourt and Ecot are no longer married, and Lefcourt bought out Ecot’s portion of the business in 2013.

The growth rate for cases sold annually hovers around 30 percent, and Lefcourt says she doesn’t see it slowing down anytime soon. She adds that about half of the growth can be attributed to increasing the number of producers in Jenny & François’s portfolio and that the other half comes from adding on- and off-premise buyers through the company’s network of distributors. Getting there, she admits, was a combination of timing, luck, and hard work.
Gaining a Foothold
“There is no way anyone today could launch a small business with such a specific vision, without investors, and turn it into a national operation the way we did in 2000,” Lefcourt says. “When we were getting established, I would actually bring a suitcase of sample bottles from wineries we wanted to import as my carry-on luggage from France to New York.”
When she landed in New York, she hit the ground running. Her father, who often picked her up at JFK, would serve as her chauffeur, driving her around Manhattan and Brooklyn so she could visit venues with her samples. Now, with so many regulations post-9/11, such a whimsical mode of operation would crumble under the strain of the TSA’s draconian Liquids Rule alone.
Lefcourt says that the initial goals she and Ecot set for the company were conservative and vague in terms of the logistics and breadth of its early imports and sales but that they were precise and rather lofty with regard to the type of wines the couple wanted to import and where they were produced.
“We only wanted wines from grapes grown by organic and biodynamic producers who also used organic methods in the cellar,” explains Lefcourt. That meant no laboratory yeasts, enzymes, sugar, artificial concentrations, acidification, or sulfites during fermentation—and no stabilizers or excess filtering or sulfites added during bottling or aging.
Wineries that hew to such stringent methods tend to focus all their resources in the vineyard and don’t usually possess splashy websites or have a staff member devoted to spreading the word on social media. To grow the Jenny & François portfolio, Lefcourt says she and Ecot needed to spend a considerable amount of time on the road, seeking out esoteric vineyards. Within a year, they realized they needed to hire a salesperson to handle the ever-increasing volume of buyers in New York.
Because as it turns out, the buyers Lefcourt met in New York loved what she had in her carry-on. “No one knew what natural wine was when we started out,” she says. “So while we were focused on the philosophy, they were just focused on the taste.”
In the early aughts, wines imported by Jenny & François landed on some of the most influential wine lists in Manhattan—including those at the revered Veritas and Gramercy Tavern—and other sommeliers took note. The couple also earned entrée almost immediately with the team at Astor Wines & Spirits, Garnet Wines & Liquors’ owner and head buyer J.R. Battipaglia, and Williamsburg’s Uva Wines & Spirits.
“[Lefcourt’s] wines were like no wines I had ever tasted before,” says Lorena Ascencios, the head wine buyer at Astor, adding that they were quirky but very good, raw but intriguing. “Without a doubt,” she says, “Jenny & François has made an indelible mark on the New York wine industry, and her wines have always sold incredibly well here at Astor.” Astor carries about 70 wines from Jenny & François at any given time—some are kept in temperature-controlled conditions to maintain stability.

Photo by Eric Medsker.
Focusing on Education
Once Lefcourt began making some headway at on- and off-premise venues, she increased her focus on education. “In 2000 the concept of natural wine didn’t really exist in the U.S., so we spent a lot of time talking about microclimates, organic-versus-conventional growing practices, and the 200 additives that are legal in winemaking but are not listed on the label,” she says, adding that the willingness of leading sommeliers and retailers to listen to what she had to say about natural wines gave her great confidence in her company’s long-term viability.
Lefcourt and Astor teamed up for more than a decade on a yearly Natural Winemakers Week, a weeklong event designed to educate consumers and members of the trade about what Ascensios describes as the “interesting but polarizing” nature of some natural wines. They eventually pulled the plug on the event when more comprehensive natural wine-tasting events—like Raw Wine—rose to prominence in the U.S.
As an importer, Jenny & François has always been extremely selective about the types of wines it imports and sells, but the selection process is not as rigid as it once was. Says Lefcourt, “We do work with winemakers who do not farm all of their grapes organically.”
Domaine de la Patience in the Costières de Nîmes, for example, had one small plot of Merlot grapes that they didn’t spray, and Lefcourt says she was moved by how delicious the wine produced from that plot was. The domaine was considering going organic, and she encouraged them to stop spraying the rest of their vineyards, which they eventually did. “I’m really happy they decided to go 100 percent organic,” says Lefcourt, “and I think it’s partially because we showed them there was a market for it. Now their wines are some of the most successful in my book, and the before-and-after difference in taste is remarkable— they’re brighter, more balanced wines.”
Changing of the Guard
In the beginning, the business took on a life of its own fairly quickly. Once Lefcourt’s selections began appearing at important restaurants and retail shops, other venues started coming to her for natural wine. Distributors in other states approached her as well, including Amy Atwood from Amy Atwood Selections in California, who, Lefcourt says, has become one of her most important partners.
  
Importer Intel
How Amy Atwood Built a Multi-Tier Natural Wine Business
The California-based importer, distributor, and producer turned her passion into a pioneering company
Lefcourt began bringing on more salespeople, averaging one every few years. Jenny & François now has five full-time sales staff members, a national sales manager, and three people to organize operations and logistics.
But during the growth of the business, her marriage faltered, Lefcourt says. She and Ecot had met during her junior year abroad, when she was enrolled as an undergraduate at Cornell. They fell in love, and after she graduated, she returned to Paris to pursue her master’s degree. She and Ecot then married. She returned to the U.S. to begin her Ph.D. program at Harvard, and the couple launched what became a global business.
“It was stressful having one home in New York and another in France,” Lefcourt says. “When we decided to separate and divorce, we tried to continue running the business together, and we did for a few years, but it became too complicated.”
A New Era
Five years ago, Lefcourt bought Ecot out. In addition to the move’s having relieved personal strain, Lefcourt says that it has simplified the business to have one person making all the final calls. In 2010, in the midst of that radical shift, Lefcourt brought on Phil Sareil to help her usher in a new era at Jenny & François.
Lefcourt had begun introducing some natural wines from Italy, Spain, and the U.S. into the portfolio, but Sareil, who had previously worked with Kermit Lynch as a regional sales manager, opened the floodgates. Over the last eight years, Sareil has added more than a dozen new wines—primarily from Central Europe—to the portfolio. “My wife is from Prague,” Sareil says, “and we spent five months together in the Czech Republic, discovering wines. For the first time, I understood how special Central European wines were.”
For winemakers like Richard Stávek, a natural wine pioneer in Moravia, with 4.5 hectares under vine, the opportunity to have his wines imported by Jenny & François has helped him grow his business significantly. “They are our first and exclusive distributor in the U.S.,” he says, “and having my wines appear on fine-dining restaurants and wine bars in New York City and Brooklyn is helping me in other markets as well.”
Sareil is particularly interested in importing natural wines from the Central European area that encompasses northeastern Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Hungary, Austria, and the Czech Republic. “When we began exploring the vineyards of [this area],” he says, referring to himself and Lefcourt, “we knew the wines would speak for themselves.”
Sareil also recently added the first cider to Jenny & François’s portfolio. It’s from a producer called Fruktstereo in Malmö, Sweden. The founder, Mikael Nypelius, praises Jenny & François for “the care and respect they have for producers and their products.”
Where will Jenny & François go next? It’s tough to say, even for Lefcourt.
“I have a six-year-old daughter,” she says of her child with her fiancé, James Robinson, “and in many ways, my approach to my child and my business is the same. I love every stage, and then looking back, I can’t believe how far we’ve come. I’ve given up on predicting what’s next, but I can’t wait to find out.”

50 Boutique Wine Importers and Distributors in the USA
29/10/2026 From specialists in natural wines and family estates to regional wholesalers serving independent retailers, these are companies wineries should know when building their U.S. distribution strategy.
For a boutique winery, the right U.S. partner does more than arrange the movement of bottles. It understands the producer, identifies suitable accounts, and gives its sales team a clear reason to recommend the wine.
That makes portfolio fit essential. A specialist in Italian family estates may be well suited to an unfamiliar indigenous variety. A natural-wine importer may place particular importance on farming and cellar practices. A regional distributor may offer the focused market coverage a small winery can realistically support.
The following guide brings together 50 boutique and specialist wine importers and distributors serving the United States. Some are small businesses with tightly focused portfolios; others are larger companies that maintain a strong commitment to independent producers.
Official websites and company portfolio information were checked for this article on October 28, 2026. This is an editorial guide, not a sales ranking. Importing and wholesale distribution are different services, and inclusion does not mean a company is currently accepting new producers.
Importers With a Strong Grower and Estate Focus
1. Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant
Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant imports wines from France and Italy, with a portfolio spanning celebrated regions and less familiar appellations. Its producer-centered approach makes it an important reference for wineries studying specialist importing. Producers should examine the existing growers and regional coverage before proposing a fit.
2. Rosenthal Wine Merchant
Rosenthal Wine Merchant emphasizes small, family-owned estates and wines that communicate their origins. Its portfolio includes producers from France, Italy, Switzerland, Spain, and Austria. For wineries, the central question is whether their vineyards, winemaking, and regional identity complement the merchant’s established approach.
3. Louis/Dressner Selections
Louis/Dressner Selections has longstanding relationships with independent growers and a strong interest in farming and winemaking practices. Its website provides extensive producer information and harvest reports. Wineries researching the business should be ready to discuss their work in the vineyard and cellar in detail.
4. Skurnik Wines & Spirits
Skurnik Wines & Spirits combines national importing with direct wholesale distribution in selected states. Its portfolio includes boutique producers from around the world. Suppliers should distinguish between a national import relationship and a proposal for a specific wholesale market, then approach the relevant team accordingly.
5. T. Edward Wines & Spirits
T. Edward Wines & Spirits began with boutique estates and continues to emphasize family-owned producers, craftsmanship, and authenticity. Its business includes importing and distribution. A winery’s introduction should explain the people behind the wine, its production philosophy, and its commercial role within the portfolio.
6. Bowler Wine
Bowler Wine is a New York-based importer and distributor focused on naturally made, small-production wines. Its selection emphasizes personality, regional character, and family growers. Wineries should research both its direct producer relationships and the other import portfolios it represents before making an introduction. NYC Wine Spirits Importer Distributor
7. European Cellars
European Cellars imports wines from family-owned properties practicing responsible viticulture. Its roots in France and Spain have expanded into other origins. Producers should assess how their wines express place and whether they add a distinct regional or stylistic contribution to the existing selection.
8. De Maison Selections
De Maison Selections is a national importer with a strong commitment to artisanal properties, regional heritage, and producer independence. Its business distinguishes national importing from direct distribution through De Maison East. Wineries should establish which relationship they are seeking before presenting their portfolio.
9. Polaner Selections
Polaner Selections combines established reference-point producers with smaller wineries, indigenous varieties, and less familiar regions. Its selection includes traditional producers and growers using organic or biodynamic practices. A compelling proposal should explain both the wine’s individuality and its value at the intended selling price.
10. Martine’s Wines
Martine’s Wines operates as an importer and wholesaler, with producer profiles and current wine information on its website. Its portfolio includes wines from established French regions and distinctive estates such as Domaine des Ardoisières. Suppliers should study the relevant regional selection before proposing additional representation. Importer & Wholesaler since 1979
Natural Wine and Small-Production Specialists
11. Jenny & François Selections
Jenny & François Selections focuses on natural wines from small growers. Its philosophy considers both vineyard practices and cellar methods. Producers researching the company should prepare a transparent account of farming, fermentation, additions, and production, alongside the practical information needed to evaluate a U.S. launch.
12. Zev Rovine Selections
Zev Rovine Selections works with growers who farm organically or biodynamically and favor minimal intervention in the cellar. Its producer list spans numerous countries. Wineries should assess philosophical fit and regional overlap, rather than assume a natural-wine identity alone creates an opening in the portfolio.
13. Selection Massale
Selection Massale imports natural wines from small wineries, emphasizing precision and drinkability. Its stated approach favors naturally fermented wines and growers working largely organically or biodynamically. Producers should explain how their practices translate into the wine’s character and consistency.
14. José Pastor Selections
José Pastor Selections champions small growers and traditionally made wines, with deep Spanish roots and a portfolio extending to other origins. Its selection includes regional grapes and distinctive vineyard environments. Wineries should explain what makes their wines an authentic expression of their particular place.
15. SelectioNaturel
SelectioNaturel specializes in Italian wines made in small quantities using natural and traditional methods. Its narrow focus makes regional and philosophical alignment especially important. Italian producers should study the represented growers and explain what their wines contribute beyond an appealing production story.
16. Vom Boden
Vom Boden focuses on small estates and growers whose work or locations sit outside the obvious mainstream. Its website includes current material on German wine. Producers considering the company should research its selection carefully and explain the vineyard, regional, and stylistic reasons their wines belong in that conversation.
17. Schatzi Wines
Schatzi Wines emphasizes the connection between growers and wine drinkers, with authenticity, sustainability, and terroir central to its approach. Its portfolio is built around producer relationships. Wineries should prepare clear information about their farming, wines, and expectations for a long-term importing partnership.
18. Olmstead Wine Co.
Olmstead Wine Co. is a Massachusetts distributor explicitly focused on natural wine. It provides a regional prospect for producers and importers whose wines fit that category. Suppliers should examine the portfolio and establish the current route for introducing new wines to the team.
19. Walden Selections
Walden Selections is a Washington State importer and distributor of wine and other beverages. It also appears in SelectioNaturel’s distribution network. Producers researching Washington should review the existing selection and discuss the specific importing or wholesale services required.
20. Nomadic Distribution
Nomadic Distribution presents itself as an importer and distributor of organic and natural wines. Its website includes producer information and a natural-wine shop. Suppliers should begin by reviewing the current producer list and confirming the relevant markets, portfolio needs, and submission process.
Regional and Country Specialists
21. The Piedmont Guy
The Piedmont Guy is a U.S.-based importer specializing in family-owned wineries from Piedmont. Its focused portfolio makes it particularly relevant to producers from that region. A pitch should explain the winery’s local identity, varieties, and position alongside the estates already represented.
22. Oliver McCrum Wines & Spirits
Oliver McCrum Wines & Spirits imports small-production Italian wines and operates distribution activities. Its stated preferences include clarity, freshness, indigenous varieties, and transparent winemaking. Producers should connect those characteristics with pricing and an account proposition that a sales team can readily explain.
23. Dalla Terra Italian Wine & Spirits
Dalla Terra describes its business as a national agent and direct importer for a select group of artisan, family-owned Italian wineries and spirits producers. Italian suppliers should understand its direct-import model and assess the existing regional portfolio before approaching the company.
24. Indigenous Selections
Indigenous Selections represents a curated group of Italian wineries selected for authenticity and regional character. Its portfolio covers origins including Piedmont, Tuscany, Veneto, Campania, Sicily, and Friuli. Producers should show how their wines offer a distinctive expression within the relevant region and price segment.
25. Porto Vino
Porto Vino maintains a French and Italian portfolio that includes producers from regions such as the Loire, Burgundy, Piedmont, and Sicily. Its website provides a detailed producer list. Suppliers should examine that regional coverage and explain where their wines add a meaningful point of difference.
26. North Berkeley Imports
North Berkeley Imports sources wines from France and Italy, combining importing with selected direct-market portfolios and distribution partners. Its offer reaches restaurants, wine shops, and collectors. Producers should distinguish the national portfolio opportunity from the company’s specific wholesale-market activities.
27. Michael Corso Selections
Michael Corso Selections is a specialist importer with a strong French wine focus. Its portfolio includes regions such as Alsace, Burgundy, the Loire, and the Rhône. Producers should present their regional credentials alongside a clear explanation of value and likely U.S. positioning.
28. Charles Neal Selections
Charles Neal Selections is a San Francisco-based importer and distributor with French wines and a substantial spirits selection. Its specialist approach makes it relevant to producers with a clear regional identity. Suppliers should explain the wine’s quality and commercial relevance without relying on small production as the sole selling point.
29. Brazos Wine Imports
Brazos Wine Imports focuses on artisan wines from Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay. Its stated interests include estate-grown, small-production wines that express specific places. South American producers should prepare detailed vineyard information and explain how the wines differ from more familiar market offerings.
30. Little Peacock Imports
Little Peacock Imports emphasizes a curated selection of family wineries, with producer listings covering Australia, France, Italy, and New Zealand. Its positioning combines discovery with commercial performance. Suppliers should explain why the wine is distinctive and how it can earn repeat purchases.
Curated Importers With Broader Portfolios
31. Grand Cru Selections
Grand Cru Selections is a New York-based importer and distributor with a strong fine-wine portfolio. Its producer information covers Champagne, Burgundy, and other regions. Wineries should research the existing estates closely and present a precise case for stylistic, regional, and commercial fit.
32. Coeur Wine Co.
Coeur Wine Co. emphasizes long-term producer relationships and wines it considers honest and authentic. Its website provides producer information and distribution partners. Suppliers should focus their introduction on the wine’s quality, its intended customer, and the practical foundations of a lasting relationship.
33. Communal Brands
Communal Brands combines production, importing, and distribution, with an emphasis on environmentally conscious wines and contemporary presentation. Its offer includes alternative formats such as boxed wine. Wineries should consider how product format, quality, and customer occasion work together within this business model.
34. Vine Connections
Vine Connections imports and distributes wines from family producers in origins including Argentina, Chile, Italy, France, and California. Its website provides trade tools such as technical sheets and shelf talkers. Producers should prepare a similarly complete set of materials when seeking representation. Global Wine, Sake & Spirits Importer
35. Massanois
Massanois is a national importer with direct distribution in selected markets. Its portfolio emphasizes quality-driven, family-owned wineries and distilleries. Suppliers should determine whether they need importing, direct wholesale distribution, or both, then tailor the proposal to the appropriate operation.
36. Banville Wine Merchants
Banville Wine Merchants combines national importing with wholesale operations in selected U.S. markets. Its approach centers on a selective, quality-focused portfolio. Producers should distinguish the national import opportunity from local distribution and identify the specific customer and price tier their wines would serve.
37. Regal Wine Imports
Regal Wine Imports maintains importing and distribution activities across wine and other beverage categories. Its website includes producer portfolios, trade information, and recent company content. Wineries should examine the relevant portfolio and market operation before proposing a new regional or stylistic addition.
38. Artisans & Vines
Artisans & Vines sources wines from Europe and several New World origins, emphasizing terroir and value. Its business includes importing, marketing, and distribution relationships. Suppliers should clarify the proposed territory and responsibilities, then connect their wine’s identity with a realistic market-development plan.
39. Wine Traditions
Wine Traditions seeks independent growers whose wines express their vineyards and offer accessible value. It operates as a national imp

How to Make It As a Small Wine Importer
As wine retailers and sommeliers continue to seek out up-and-coming regions, the number of small, independent importers is booming. Megan Krigbaum on how these "little guys" are changing the market, and how they got started.
story:  Megan Krigbaum
photo: Lizzie Munro
camille riviere small wine importers  
 Share story:
 Share
 Tweet
 
 Email
When I was first getting into wine, I, like many before me, became an avid player of Spin the Bottle. At tastings, in wine shops, at restaurant tables, I was constantly turning wines around to see the back label. This game of investigation revealed the importer, giving subtle clues about the style of what was in the bottle. And for a good stretch, I felt pretty in the loop with the small guys: Kermit Lynch and Neal Rosenthal, traditional French and Italian wines with purity; Louis/Dressner, avant-garde naturalist producers; De Maison Selections, off-the-beaten path discoveries from Spain; Rare Wine Co., seminal Old World winemakers.
But then, starting a handful of years ago, I found that more often than not when I’d spin, I’d come full-stop: Who the hell is that? Names that I’d never seen before, like Zev Rovine, José Pastor, Acid Inc. and, more recently, Selection Massale, Camille Rivière and Coeur Wine Co., were inhabiting a substantial amount of shelf and wine list space—each a small but mighty presence. Not only were the importers new to me, but the wines and producers were, too.
Whereas, ten or 15 years ago, to be small meant anything other than Southern Wine & Spirits and its behemoth brethren, in today’s Golden Era of imports, that scale is much wider, with big at one end and small, smaller, smallest at the other. Largely, the success of these smaller businesses stems from intensely committed buyers at both the restaurant and retail level, an ever-growing interest in natural and more obscure wines and, crucially, a few importing logistics companies—like T. Elenteny and Fruit of the Vines—that are helping to make importing small amounts of wine much easier by handling administrative services for freight, customs and shipping.
> After the honeymoon period of discovering those first wines, the dream model—fly to France, rent a car, knock on doors, find the next Coche-Dury—so perfectly set forth by Kermit Lynch’s Adventures on the Wine Route is hardly a reality.
“There’s been a real rise in sommeliers that are into off-the-beaten-path regions and retailers that champion smaller producers,” says Eric Clemons, owner of Coeur Wine Co., which imports wines from France, Italy and Spain exclusively to New York and New Jersey. That these buyers are receptive to working with a large swath of suppliers—some sommeliers say they buy from 40 or 50 different importers in a year—is a sea change from the way things used to be, whenrestaurants and stores relied on just a few importers. The smartest buyers see the opportunity found in this diversity, despite the extra work.
“[Small importers] have continued to bring me new discoveries from almost-forgotten corners of Italy,” says Shelley Lindgren, of Italian restaurants A16 and SPQR in San Francisco.  “I was lucky to find the three Etna Rossos we carried when we first opened; now, we carry dozens of excellent styles and producers from Mt. Etna.”
The crazy thing is that Etna feels almost mainstream at this point, which sits these new upstarts in a bit of an arms race to find the next great region and as-yet-unknown producers for discovery-hungry buyers before anyone else does. Plenty are placing bets on the Savoie and southwest France, while other are looking to producers who are upsetting the status quo in places like Chile and South Africa.
Yet no matter how intense the competition has become, the model still holds that if you’re going to be a wine importer, you will probably find your start in a couple of bottles that you bring home in your suitcase from Europe. That’s how Jenny Lefcourt launched her natural wine-focused company, Jenny & François Selections, back in 2000 while studying in France.
“I fell upon a little tasting in the Loire, the Dive Bouteille, which at the time was probably only ten or 15 producers,” says Lefcourt. “Now, that same tasting has grown to over 100 producers, with thousands of people around the world coming to taste.”
She realized years ago that the natural movement had expanded outside France, so she expanded her business, too. Jenny & Francois now brings in more than 60 producers from Italy, Spain, Austria and, most recently, the Czech Republic—from areas that produce the sort of cool-climate, high acid wines Lefcourt has always chased since she first fell in love with Loire Valley whites.
But after the honeymoon period of discovering those first wines, the dream model—fly to France, rent a car, knock on doors, find the next Coche-Dury—so perfectly set forth by Kermit Lynch’s Adventures on the Wine Route is hardly a reality. Importing and distributing wine requires a huge sum of money up front, patience to wade through the thicket of United States importation laws and an unwavering commitment to pounding the pavement to sell wine.
“People get confused as to what they’re doing in the wine business,” says André Tamers of De Maison Selections, which is celebrating 20 years of business. “They think starting a distribution company is about going to Europe and having lunch, but it’s about having a truck.”
Fifteen years into this importing revolution, these new little guys keep turning up with new places, winemakers and wines. And at this moment when there’s a new portfolio popping up every couple of months, it only stands to reason that Spin the Bottle will become more of a stats game, along the lines of knowing a baseball player’s batting average and all the teams he’s ever played for. But it does seem that this new crop will continue to push all aspects of the industry for the better. “The little guys keep us one our toes,” says Tamers. “We’re making a newer, better website and always looking over our shoulder to make sure were in the right places.”
Here, five importers who have gotten their start in the last ten years, and what they’ve learned in the process.
AI Selections
Location: New York City and 14 states  
Who: David Weitzenhoffer and Laura Supper
David Weitzenhoffer, a former wine director at NYC’s Felidia, launched this company with Laura Supper (a coworker at the restaurant) in 2007, after spending several months in Piedmont and realizing that there were a lot of great wines that just weren’t making their way to the States. He started out by bringing in obscure varieties, like refosco, and obscure regional wines, like Rosso Conero, and sold them mostly to restaurant contacts. Weitzenhoffer figures his company is a little bigger than small at this point—with 20 salespeople selling 60-some producers in 14 states. This growth has brought its own new level of competition: “Until you’re a certain size, you’re irrelevant to the larger importers, who want something that they can scale.” Only recently have other importers started to show interest in his producers. His first import, Vignai da Duline from Friuli—a producer Weitzenhoffer describes as “the blueprint for wineries he wanted to work with”—recently went to none other than Kermit Lynch.
Calling-Card Wines: High-elevation Chianti Classico from Monteraponi, high-acid whites from Zidarich in Friuli and Van Volxem in the Mosel, ruché and barbera from Dino and Paolo Dacapo in Piedmont.
Avant Garde Wine & Spirits
Location: New York City  
Who: Geoffroy Ducroux
Paris-born Geoffroy Ducroux only sells his wines in New York City—“The goal is to always be a direct importer, not to sell to distributors in other states,” he says. As a one-man team, he’s able to run his business out of a WeWork shared office space near Madison Square Park and visit all of his clients personally. On a good day, he’ll have six or seven appointments, riding on the NYC bus system from one to the next. Ducroux worked in sales for importer Domaine Select for ten years before quitting, heading to France for a month and coming home with a dozen producers onboard for his new importing business. He’s confident he started at the exact right moment: “If I’d waited another year, I wouldn’t have found as many producers with such pedigree and such a following, like Benoit Courault in Anjou,” he says. Now, it’s harder to find these small greats because so many other people are on the same hunt; some of his biggest discoveries have come from following blogs and French newspapers, rather than spending loads of time in Europe.
Calling-Card Wines:Vivid Burgundies from rising star Fanny Sabre in the Côte de Beaune, cremants and focused whites from Alsace’s Valentin Zusslin, grower Champagne from Vouette et Sorbée in the Aube.
Camille Rivière Selection
Location: New York City  
Who: Camille Rivière
After managing high-end accounts for mega importer Frederick Wildman for five years, Rivière called it quits to go home to France and rejigger her life. While on vacation, she discovered natural wines for the first time and spent the next two years absorbed in vineyards around the country. Since 2012, she’s pulled together a portfolio comprised of a couple dozen teensy natural producers. “I’ve had distributors from Arizona, Michigan, etc., say ‘We want to distribute your wine,’ but I don’t even have enough for my clients in New York,” says Rivière. “My dad said to me, ‘Why don’t you bring in bigger domaines?’ But if I do that, I’ll lose all legitimacy.” Finding the right producers she wants to work with isn’t the difficult part—she’s in France tasting a couple times a year—but what she struggles with most is sussing out the buyers that she thinks will do a great job with her wines. When prospective buyers reach out, she makes sure “that they have temperature-controlled storage, that they have people on staff who can talk about these wines and that they don’t have ridiculous markups.”
Calling-Card Wines:Affordable reds from Languedoc’s Clos Fantine and Mas Coutelou, Jura cult favorites from Stéphane Tissot.
Coeur Wine Co.
Location: New York City and New Jersey  
Who: Eric Clemons
After working up the ranks at importer Skurnik wines for ten years (Skurnik, over the past 25 years, has spawned numerous others, including Polaner, David Bowler and, most recently, Schatzi), Clemons launched Coeur in 2014. “When Kermit Lynch and Neal Rosenthal started their companies, they didn’t have the internet. They had to be fluent in French and knocking on doors. But now it’s so much easier to be in touch with people from the far corners of the world.” Today’s competitive arena makes it so that it’s important for Clemons to constantly be in the market selling (he only has two other salespeople). He relies a lot on the advice of his producers when it comes to picking up new ones. “When you work with a person that you really like and trust, it’s really valuable when they send someone your way,” says Clemons. He’s found that a lot of producers he’s connected with are around his age (33) and taking over the reins from their parents.
Calling-Card Wines:Biodynamic, old-vine Beaujolais from Yann Bertrand, outstanding chenin blanc from Saumur-Champigny’s Chteau Yvonne, sherry from the nearly 200-year-old Bodegas Gutiérrez Colosía.
Selection Massale
Location: San Francisco and New York City  
Who: Cory Cartwright and Guilhaume Gerard
In 2009, Cory Cartwright left his career as a video game designer to team up with Guilhaume Gerard, who, at the time, was an owner of Terroir wine bar in San Francisco, to start what began as a direct-to-consumer wine importing company. The two changed that model to mainly sell wholesale after quickly realizing how big the demand was for natural wines from small producers. Cartwright says that selling wine, in general, has changed: Buyers don’t want to work with big companies and salespeople in suits—they want to have a personal relationship. Same goes for the producers; with each one, he and Gerard “have been to their homes, spent days with them, know their kids and their husbands and wives, tasted the wines on site.”
Calling-Card Wines:Pét-nats from the Loire’s Frantz Saumon, vibrant Chinons from Jérôme Lenoir, Burgundies from cult favorite Céline and Laurent Tripoz and the sensational alpine wines of Domaine Belluard.
Photo: Camille Rivière in her home/office.

Partners
Wine Traditions
Foundational for Ed and Barbara, the owners, has been the belief that the meaningful expression of land is not limited to a small group of anointed appellations. Over the last two and half decades, the wine selection has been guided by principles similar to those attributed to the architect, Albert Frey; economy, discipline, functionalism, and beauty. As the portfolio has evolved, so has our understanding of the wine traditions of France. They are “rooted” in the land and brought forward through the cultivation and preservation of the vineyards for future generations. The “organic habit of re-creating what has been received and is handed on” allows the perceptive vigneron or vigneronne to give the land a powerful voice through the wines they produce. Their passion inspires us.
Learn More
Portovino
For over 20 years, we’ve been traveling Italy’s backroads to create a collection of terroir-driven wines that excite us: characterful daily-drinkers, heritage producers, and fringe outliers. In 2021, we added a small German & Austrian portfolio from producers we’ve been friends with over the years.
All are certified organic, biodynamic, or practicing organic with a list of best practices. We don’t work with large scale commercial wineries, and we don’t peddle wines from tank farms to keep the lights on (there are smarter, more environmentally interesting ways to keep the lights on!).
Learn More
Field Recordings
Field Recordings is winemaker Andrew Jones’ personal catalog of the people and places he values most. Our wines are all about the flavor — with none of the pretension.
Spending his days as a vine nursery fieldman planning and planting vineyards for farmers all over California, Andrew is sometimes offered small lots of their best fruit on the side. Having stood in just about every vineyard on the Central Coast, he’s all about finding those underdogs with untapped potential. As friendships are made and opportunities are embraced, Andrew produces small quantities of soulful wine from these unusual, quiet vineyards.
Learn More
Baobab Wines
Baobab Wines was founded in 2015 with the mission to bring the best of South Africa to the United States. Frustrated with the export driven South African brands that overwhelmed the US wine market we sought out family owned and operated Vineyards from each appellation with a commitment to tell the true story of the South African wine industry – our history, our terroir, our culture, and what is driving the future of winemaking in South Africa.

results.rawContent:
Natural wine for wine distributors and importers: complete 2026 guide
Editorial Team @ 2026-11-09 14:51:37 -0800
For wine distributors and importers, natural wine sourcing is the process of selecting and qualifying wines with the aim of building a portfolio that earns repeat orders. This 2026 guide covers producer checks, tasting, territory agreements, and account support—because a compelling bottle still needs accurate records and a clear route to market.
Natural wine distributors should verify each wine, vintage, and territory before making portfolio commitments.
Tinto Amorio suits buyers seeking California natural wine; assess individual wines and wholesale terms separately.
Importers need destination-specific documentation, not assumptions drawn from a winery’s consumer storefront.
Build account support around tasting notes, service guidance, and repeat orders—not unsupported health claims.
Why natural wine sourcing matters for distributors and importers
Your job is to qualify the wine and the commercial relationship separately. A great tasting does not establish territory rights. A polished product page does not establish import eligibility. Keep those decisions separate until both pass review.
Tinto Amorio makes natural, orange, organic, and low-sulfite wines in California and sells wholesale to bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars across 18 US states. That existing wholesale footprint gives buyers a concrete reason to discuss account fit; it does not establish representation rights in any particular territory.
Natural wine also requires precise language. Organic, biodynamic, skin contact, and low-sulfite describe different attributes, not interchangeable promises. Record the evidence for each claim against the exact wine you intend to represent.
For your 2026 sourcing plan, use 3 account types as separate planning lanes: bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars. Ask what each buyer needs to explain, serve, and reorder the wine. Then work backward to the producer information required to support that sale.
How to qualify natural wine for your portfolio
Define the account need before choosing the wine
Start with a spreadsheet and conversations with your existing buyers. Record the role the new wine must fill: an introduction to skin-contact wine, a food-focused listing, or a specialist bottle-shop selection. A style name alone is not a buying brief.
Ask buyers what they struggle to explain at the shelf or table. Distinguish a request for a particular taste from a request for a farming or production claim. Someone asking for organic wine has a different qualification question from someone asking for more texture.
Write a short acceptance brief before requesting samples. Keep it specific enough that another member of your team can use it without hearing the producer’s pitch.
Name the target account type and intended service format.
Describe the desired acidity, texture, tannin, and aromatic character.
Identify which production claims require supporting documents.
State whether the wine fills a gap or replaces an existing listing.
Record the buyer objections your sales team must answer.
Verify the exact wine and market record
Build a shared folder manually before investing in a larger catalog system. Give each wine a record that separates producer statements, supporting documents, and your own tasting observations. Never let a tasting note become evidence of certification.
For natural wine distributors, vintage control deserves its own check. A winery can release a familiar label with different grapes or production details. An older export listing is not a substitute for the current record covering the wine you will receive.
In 2026, date every approved sales sheet and identify its intended market. If a fact is unresolved, leave it out of customer-facing copy until the producer confirms it. Missing detail is easier to correct than a claim already repeated across accounts.
Match the product name, vintage, and destination market.
Request the current technical sheet and label artwork.
Verify certification claims against applicable supporting documents.
Ask for exact wording on sulfites, additives, and production methods.
Assign an owner to replace outdated sales materials.
Contact the producer with a qualified brief
Use a short email rather than a broad request for everything the winery makes. Explain your territory, account mix, current portfolio gap, and purchasing role. Distinguish distribution, importation, and individual wholesale buying at the start.
Tinto Amorio is best for buyers seeking California natural wine for bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars. Its existing wholesale business makes it relevant to that brief. Territory rights, technical documentation, and account terms still need direct confirmation.
A focused producer conversation is the faster path once your brief is ready. Instead of assembling a commercial proposal from consumer pages, request the documents and contacts needed for your exact market. Do not interpret an online checkout as a wholesale agreement.
Introduce your legal business name and operating territory.
Describe the accounts you serve and the portfolio role you need.
Clarify whether you seek import rights, distribution rights, or wholesale purchasing.
Request current trade documents for the wines under discussion.
Ask who owns technical, commercial, and logistics questions.
Taste for the intended account and service conditions
Run an initial tasting with consistent glassware, written notes, and the same evaluation prompts for every sample. Describe what you taste before discussing the producer story. This keeps an attractive narrative from replacing sensory judgment.
Plan 2 tasting sessions as an internal evaluation method: an initial assessment and a separate account-service assessment. This is a proposed buying process, not a shelf-life benchmark. Follow the producer’s handling guidance and record the conditions used.
For the second assessment, reproduce the intended service setting. A restaurant buyer needs to understand how a wine works alongside food; a bottle-shop team needs language customers can use at home. Record differences without automatically treating every unusual aroma or cloudy appearance as either a virtue or a fault.
Use the results to write a short sales explanation. For a Tinto Amorio natural wine review, keep your sensory notes distinct from the winery’s verified production facts. Neither should silently replace the other.
Record aroma, acidity, texture, tannin, and finish.
Note sample identity, opening time, and service conditions.
Assess food fit against the intended account’s menu.
Separate personal preference from faults requiring investigation.
Write a plain-language explanation for the eventual customer.
Confirm territory, responsibilities, and handling
Start with a responsibility sheet that names who does what. Separate the producer, importer, distributor, warehouse, carrier, and buying account where those parties apply. Do not assume that a familiar shipping arrangement covers a new market.
US importers should check applicable federal requirements with the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau and confirm state obligations with the relevant authorities. For other destinations, check the destination’s requirements. Have qualified advisers resolve legal questions before goods move.
Keep your 2026 territory record separate from general brand coverage. A producer’s presence in a state does not tell you who holds representation rights there. Put the scope of the relationship in writing, including who approves changes to labels and trade materials.
Confirm the permitted territory and any exclusivity terms.
Identify responsibility for permits, approvals, and documentation.
Record producer-specified transport and storage conditions.
Agree on inspection, damage reporting, and escalation responsibilities.
Document how vintage changes reach your sales and operations teams.
Launch with account training and a reorder review
Use a shared account tracker first. Connect each placement to its buyer, staff briefing, approved description, and follow-up owner. The goal is a repeatable account relationship, not a list of opening orders.
Train staff to explain what is in the glass before asking them to tell a long production story. Give them a sensory sentence, a food or occasion cue, and the verified facts behind any category claim. Keep health promises out of the pitch.
Use the natural wine wholesale account onboarding guide to structure the handoff. For your 2026 review, examine repeat orders, unresolved service questions, and the reasons buyers decline—not just the number of accounts approached.
Supply approved descriptions tied to the exact wine.
Brief staff on service and handling instructions.
Record account feedback in the buyer’s own words.
Track initial placements separately from repeat orders.
Assign a follow-up action to each unresolved objection.
Compare sourcing options for your business
Choose a sourcing route by responsibility and account fit, not by how direct it sounds. Direct producer contact gives you a focused conversation, but it does not remove regulatory work. A broader portfolio creates more choice, but each wine still needs qualification.
These options describe relationships to assess, not confirmed commercial arrangements. In particular, a consumer product listing does not establish the terms of a trade relationship.
Option,Best for,Main advantage,Key limitation
Direct winery relationship, including Tinto Amorio,Buyers assessing a focused California natural wine producer,Direct discussion of the wines and producer records,Territory, documentation, and commercial responsibilities require separate confirmation
Existing in-market importer or distributor,Licensed accounts seeking a local trade relationship,A local contact for the represented portfolio,Selection and representation are bounded by that business’s agreements
Direct import relationship,Importers seeking a producer relationship for a destination market,Direct coordination with the producer,The importer must establish applicable obligations and operating responsibilities
Multi-producer portfolio sourcing,Distributors filling several distinct account needs,More stylistic options to assess,More records, training materials, and producer relationships to maintain

A direct winery relationship is not automatically the right choice for every buyer. Match the route to the work your business is equipped to perform. If your team cannot own a required responsibility, identify a qualified partner before proceeding.
Common mistakes distributors and importers make
Treating natural as proof of every production claim
Natural wine is not a substitute for a wine-specific evidence file. Do not infer organic certification, vegan suitability, or sulfite content from the category name. Approve each statement separately and retain the supporting record.
Reusing facts across vintages and markets
A familiar label can make an old technical sheet look safe to reuse. Check the exact wine, vintage, and destination before publishing a new sales sheet. Mark superseded files clearly so account teams do not keep circulating them.
Confusing consumer sales with trade permissions
A winery’s consumer storefront does not establish distribution rights, import eligibility, or your right to represent the brand. Confirm the commercial relationship separately. Keep permission records alongside the territory brief rather than buried in email.
Selling the story without a service explanation
A farming story does not tell restaurant staff how to describe texture or help a shopper choose dinner. Give accounts a plain-language taste description and verified handling guidance. Test whether a staff member can explain the wine without repeating a paragraph of jargon.
Calling a placement a successful launch
An opening order establishes a placement, not a repeat-order pattern. Ask what happened after the first staff tasting and customer conversations. Use those answers to adjust account support before expanding the same approach elsewhere.
FAQ
What should natural wine distributors check before taking on a producer?
Natural wine distributors should check account fit, wine-specific records, territory rights, and operating responsibilities. Assess the tasting and the commercial relationship separately before committing.
What is the difference between a natural wine importer and a distributor?
An importer brings wine into a destination country, while a distributor supplies wine within an authorized market. One business can perform both roles when properly authorized; confirm the responsibilities for the particular transaction.
Is Tinto Amorio a fit for a natural wine distribution portfolio?
Tinto Amorio is a fit to assess for buyers seeking California natural wine for bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars. The winery sells wholesale across 18 US states, but territory rights and individual account terms require direct confirmation.
Does natural wine mean the wine is certified organic?
No, the term natural wine does not by itself establish organic certification. Request supporting documentation for the exact wine and use only the claims that documentation supports.
Can I use the same technical sheet for every vintage?
Use the same technical sheet only when the producer confirms it applies to the exact wine and vintage. Keep market-specific records separate and replace superseded documents in your sales materials.
How should importers evaluate natural wine samples?
Importers should evaluate samples against the intended account, using consistent tasting prompts and recorded service conditions. Keep sensory observations separate from verified production facts and investigate suspected faults with the producer.
Can a restaurant buy directly from a winery instead of a distributor?
Direct winery purchasing depends on the applicable jurisdiction and the parties’ permissions. Confirm the rules for the specific transaction rather than assuming a consumer checkout establishes a lawful wholesale route.
One last thing
Ask a colleague who missed the producer meeting to explain the wine from your sales sheet. If the colleague cannot distinguish how it tastes from how it was made, rewrite the sheet. That small test exposes the gap between an engaging producer story and information an account can actually use.

results.rawContent:
Westwood Estate WineryWestwood Estate Winery

A Certified Biodynamic and Organic Vineyard. Sustainability is at the core of our soil and our soul.
Every wine we make begins with Biodynamic, Organic, and Sustainable fruit. Sustaining the land, animals, and the team that makes our wine possible is the foundation of our culture. It’s the “How” to the question of “How we make Unforgettable Wines.” You see it in the way we treat each other, our supplier-partners, our fellow farmer-winemakers, and our community. And you see it in the way we treat our lands.
We believe these farming practices not only enhance the health of the land but also allow us to create natural wines that are pure expressions of their home. Wines of character come from soils with healthy biomes that form a balanced ecosystem with the vine and nourish it with flavors most natural to the vineyard.
Our mission to create unforgettable wines begins right here on our home vineyard, the Annadel Gap Vineyard. An unexpected gem of a vineyard on the northern edge of the Sonoma Valley that we discovered over twenty years ago. And we have a very special place in the Sonoma Valley’s Annadel Gap – thirty-three unique acres.
We farm Biodynamically and Organically.
We farm Biodynamically and Organically.
After a painstaking multi-year process, we were awarded Demeter Biodynamic certification in 2016 and CCOF Organic certification in 2017. Every grape grown on our Annadel Gap Estate is certified Demeter Biodynamic and CCOF Organic – carefully tended with the most eco-responsible methods available.
Biodynamics is the highest level of organic farming – Organic squared! Developed in the 1920s by Dr. Rudolf Steiner, Biodynamics treats the vineyard as a single living organism. Eliminating synthetic fertilizers and pesticides is the beginning, but Biodynamics goes further, encouraging extreme biodiversity, a closed nutrient system, the use of natural “teas” and a personal connection to the land. In harmony with the lunar cycle, Steiner believed this discipline results in a self-sustaining cycle of living and higher energy to the fruit.
Since our transition to Biodynamics, our vines have become stronger, more disease-resistant, and the roots have deepened dramatically – now requiring virtually no irrigation. Our vineyard is healthy and balanced, and wildlife – jackrabbits and toads especially – are super-abundant. And we swear, you can sense the higher energy in the place and the wines!
Today, we are one of a handful of Demeter-certified Biodynamic vineyards in North America. Why don’t more people do it? It’s expensive. Between the physical workload and lower yields from the vines, costs can be 50%-100% greater than with conventional farming. However, it is catching on fast! Virtually all Grand Cru Burgundy producers farm Biodynamically and are being closely followed by the top-tier producers in Bordeaux and around the world.
Cared for by a Biodynamic legend.
Cared for by a Biodynamic legend.
Philippe Coderey is a legend in the natural, Organic, and Biodynamic viticulture field. Philippe serves as our Biodynamic Vineyard Consultant, leading the viticulture team to implement the Biodynamic and Organic practices across the whole vineyard. Philippe’s last name comes from the French verb, “couderer,” which means to cultivate vineyards. He grew up on vineyards in Provençe, learning traditional and natural viticultural techniques from elders. He puts all of his passion and knowledge to work in our vineyards.
We are partners with our land.
We believe we are stewards of the land. It’s only ours for a little while, and then it is someone else’s honor to tend to it. We are pesticide-free and herbicide-free. We follow the cycles of nature (check out our calendar below), sowing cover crops to protect the soil and attract beneficial bugs. Our hand-crafted wines begin right here in the vineyard, with our hand-made, nutrient-dense Biodynamic sprays and organic composts, all applied by hand.

Our rewards are many.
Our rewards are many.
We are rewarded with prospering vines and a variety of wildlife calling our estate their home. We are rewarded by the health of labor and the richness of being close to the earth. And we are rewarded with grapes that make opulent, distinctive, and unforgettable wines.
